questions.q: List the four regulatory mechanisms that characterised the pre-1991 industrial sector in India as described in the NCERT textbook.
questions.a: The four mechanisms were: (i) industrial licensing for starting/closing firms and deciding output, (ii) private sector barred from many industries, (iii) certain goods reserved exclusively for small-scale industries, (iv) government controls on price fixation and distribution of selected industrial products. A wrong answer (e.g., mentioning only licensing) reveals the student has not internalised the multi-dimensional nature of the pre-reform regulatory architecture — they see one tool instead of a system of controls.

questions.q: Why did the government retain industrial licensing for alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, and drugs & pharmaceuticals after 1991? Explain the economic rationale for each category.
questions.a: Licensing was retained for: (a) alcohol & cigarettes — demerit goods with negative externalities (health costs), requiring quantity control; (b) hazardous chemicals & industrial explosives — public safety and environmental risks needing strict monitoring; (c) electronics & aerospace — strategic sectors with defence implications and technology sensitivity; (d) drugs & pharmaceuticals — public health criticality, quality assurance, and price affordability concerns. A wrong answer that says "these are profitable sectors" reveals a confusion between economic rationale (market failure/strategic interest) and commercial viability — the student is applying a profit motive where the state acts to correct externalities or protect security.

questions.q: Using the NCERT Table 3.1 data, calculate the average annual industrial growth rate for the periods 1980-91 and 1992-2001. Then explain why the growth rate decreased despite liberalisation.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify industrial growth rates from Table 3.1: 1980-91 = 7.1%, 1992-2001 = 6.5%. Step 2: Compute average (already given as period averages). Step 3: The decline from 7.1% to 6.5% occurred because: (i) cheaper imports replaced domestic demand (import liberalisation), (ii) inadequate infrastructure investment (power, transport) raised production costs, (iii) global competition exposed inefficiencies of protected firms, (iv) cyclical downturn in early 1990s. A wrong answer that claims "liberalisation always raises growth immediately" reveals a misunderstanding of transition costs — the student ignores the J-curve effect where restructuring, competitive shakeout, and infrastructure gaps cause short-term slowdown before efficiency gains materialise.

questions.q: Compare the pre-1991 and post-1991 industrial policy on the dimension of "firm size and scale". How did dereservation of SSI goods affect economies of scale and market structure?
questions.a: Pre-1991: Many goods (e.g., garments, toys, leather products) reserved for SSI — firms legally prevented from expanding beyond investment limits, forcing artificial smallness and preventing economies of scale. Post-1991: Progressive dereservation (e.g., 2005: 500+ items dereserved) allowed firms to grow, adopt modern technology, achieve minimum efficient scale, and compete globally. Market structure shifted from fragmented small firms to more consolidated, scale-efficient units — but also caused displacement of traditional SSI units unable to upgrade. A wrong answer focusing only on "employment loss in SSI" reveals a static view — the student misses the dynamic trade-off: short-term dislocation vs long-term productivity and export competitiveness (e.g., India's garment exports surged post-dereservation).

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Abolition of industrial licensing was sufficient to create a competitive industrial sector in India." Use evidence from the NCERT text on infrastructure, import competition, and market access.
questions.a: The statement is false. Licensing removal was necessary but not sufficient. NCERT highlights: (i) Infrastructure inadequacy (power, transport) persisted due to low investment — raising costs for domestic firms, (ii) Cheaper imports flooded the market (quantitative restrictions removed, tariffs reduced) — domestic demand shifted to foreign goods, (iii) Developed countries maintained non-tariff barriers (e.g., USA quota on Indian textiles) — Indian firms couldn't access foreign markets symmetrically. Thus, domestic firms faced "competition without competitiveness" — exposed to imports but lacking infrastructure and market access to compete globally. A wrong answer that says "yes, licensing removal created competition" reveals a one-reform fallacy — the student treats a single policy lever as a magic bullet, ignoring complementary reforms needed in infrastructure, trade symmetry, and factor markets.

questions.q: Design a policy brief for a state government that wants to attract manufacturing investment in 2024. Incorporate three lessons from India's 1991 industrial licensing abolition and two caveats from the post-reform experience.
questions.a: Lessons: (1) Remove entry permits — replace with simple registration/online single-window clearance. (2) Allow market-determined prices — no state price controls on outputs. (3) Open to private/foreign capital — no sectoral bans except strategic. Caveats: (1) Pair deregulation with parallel infrastructure investment (power, logistics, water) — otherwise firms face high operating costs. (2) Ensure trade policy symmetry — if you open to imports, negotiate market access for exports; otherwise local firms get squeezed. A poor answer that copies 1991 measures verbatim without adapting to 2024 context (e.g., ignoring environmental clearances, labour codes, digital infrastructure) reveals inability to transfer principles across time — the student memorises history but cannot apply institutional economics to new settings.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Industrial sector ______ refers to the systematic dismantling of government controls — specifically the abolition of industrial licensing (except for a few strategic sectors), removal of entry barriers for private and foreign capital, dereservation of small-scale industries, and market-determined pricing — to replace a permit-raj regime with competitive market forces that allocate resources based on efficiency and consumer demand.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you want to start a bicycle ______ unit in 1985: you needed a licence from Delhi bureaucrats specifying how many bicycles you could produce, where to locate, and whether you could expand — even if customers demanded more.
What is Industrial sector liberalisation? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Industrial sector liberalisation refers to the systematic dismantling of government controls — specifically the abolition of industrial licensing (except for a few strategic sectors), removal of entry barriers for private and foreign capital, dereservation of small-scale industries, and market-determined pricing — to replace a permit-raj.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Now, picture the same decision in ______: no licence required, you decide output based on market demand, and you can import better technology freely.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the removal of industrial licensing altered firm entry/exit decisions, calculate the change in number of reserved industries using pre- and post-1991 data, and evaluate the impact on domestic competition using the concepts of barriers to entry, economies of scale, and contestable markets.
